title: Foundational Document on the College of Fabricators

sections.title: Definition
sections.body: The College of Fabricators is a peer body of practitioners skilled in the working of materials—welding, machining, metal forming, and woodworking. Its purpose is to maintain standards of practice, transmit knowledge to new practitioners, supply qualified members for sortition to manufacturing oversight committees, and exercise governance authority over the Manufacturing Service's fabrication functions as delegated by the General Assembly.
sections.rationale: Fabrication is fundamental to a community's material self-sufficiency. The College ensures that the community maintains genuine competence in these essential skills.

sections.title: Domain
sections.body: The College's domain includes: welding (arc, MIG, TIG, oxy-acetylene), machining (lathe, mill, drill press, grinder), metal forming (bending, cutting, shaping), woodworking (joinery, finishing, furniture-making), tool maintenance and safety, and workshop operations. The domain may expand as the College develops capacity in additional fabrication disciplines.
sections.rationale: Clear domain definition prevents scope creep while allowing organic growth as practitioners develop new skills.

sections.title: Relationship to Services
sections.body: Members of the College of Fabricators may work in the Manufacturing Service, Housing Service construction functions, or any other Service requiring fabrication skills. College membership is not required for Service employment. College membership places a practitioner in the qualified sortition pool for governance functions requiring fabrication expertise.
sections.rationale: Separating civic credentials from employment prevents the College from becoming a closed shop while maintaining its governance function.

sections.title: Eligibility
sections.body: Membership is open to any Society member who demonstrates competence in one or more fabrication disciplines within the College's domain. Competence may be demonstrated through: work product review by existing members, supervised practice assessment, completion of apprenticeship under a College member, or documented professional experience.
sections.rationale: Multiple pathways to membership recognize that fabrication skills can be developed through formal training, apprenticeship, or independent practice.

sections.title: Peer Assessment
sections.body: Existing College members assess applicants' work and determine whether it meets the standards of safe and competent practice in the relevant discipline. Assessment focuses on technical skill, safety awareness, and quality of work rather than speed or efficiency.
sections.rationale: Peers are best positioned to recognize genuine competence. Safety emphasis prevents the College from credentialing practitioners who pose risks to themselves or others.

sections.title: Safety Requirement
sections.body: All members must demonstrate understanding of basic shop safety, tool operation safety, material hazards, and emergency procedures. Safety knowledge is non-negotiable for membership.
sections.rationale: Fabrication work involves inherent hazards. The College has a duty to the community to ensure its members practice safely.

sections.title: Specialization
sections.body: Members need not be competent in all fabrication disciplines to join the College. A welder, a machinist, and a woodworker bring different skills. All are members. When the Assembly draws from the College for a committee requiring specific fabrication expertise, the draw may be limited to members credentialed in the relevant discipline.
sections.rationale: Recognizing specialization within a broad college allows the community to develop deep expertise in specific disciplines while maintaining a unified fabrication peer body.

sections.title: Apprenticeship
sections.body: The College encourages members to take apprentices and transmit their skills to new practitioners. Successful completion of apprenticeship under a College member is a recognized path to membership. The College may establish apprenticeship standards but shall not make formal apprenticeship the only path to membership.
sections.rationale: Apprenticeship preserves knowledge transmission traditions while preventing gatekeeping through excessive formalization.

sections.title: Standards of Practice
sections.body: The College maintains written standards of safe and competent practice for each fabrication discipline within its domain. Standards shall be accessible to all members and shall be revised as technology and practice evolve. Standards serve as teaching tools and quality benchmarks, not as rigid rules.
sections.rationale: Documented standards prevent knowledge loss and provide clear guidance for new practitioners while allowing experienced members to exercise judgment.

sections.title: Tool and Workshop Knowledge
sections.body: The College holds institutional knowledge about tool selection, maintenance, workshop setup, and equipment operation. This knowledge shall be documented and made available to the Manufacturing Service, Housing Service, and other community functions that maintain fabrication capacity.
sections.rationale: Communities often lose tool knowledge when experienced practitioners leave or retire. The College prevents this loss by maintaining institutional memory.

sections.title: Knowledge Sharing
sections.body: College members shall actively share knowledge with apprentices, interested community members, and each other. The College may organize skill-sharing sessions, tool demonstrations, and collaborative projects. Fabrication knowledge is a community resource, not private property.
sections.rationale: Mutual aid societies thrive on knowledge sharing. Hoarding expertise undermines the College's purpose.

sections.title: Innovation and Adaptation
sections.body: The College encourages members to develop new techniques, adapt tools and processes to community needs, and experiment with materials and methods. Innovation shall be documented and shared rather than kept as individual trade secrets.
sections.rationale: Small communities need practitioners who can adapt and improvise. Encouraging innovation while requiring documentation builds collective capacity.

sections.title: Manufacturing Service Oversight
sections.body: When the General Assembly establishes a committee to oversee the Manufacturing Service's fabrication functions, it shall draw members from the College of Fabricators. The College does not govern the Manufacturing Service directly—that authority comes from the Assembly's delegation to the drawn committee.
sections.rationale: Qualified sortition ensures that people with actual fabrication expertise oversee fabrication work, while maintaining democratic legitimacy through random selection from a credentialed pool.

sections.title: Safety Standards
sections.body: The College may be delegated authority by the Assembly to establish safety standards for fabrication work across all Services. Safety standards developed by the College shall be binding on all community fabrication operations.
sections.rationale: Safety expertise should be centralized and consistently applied. The College is the natural body to hold this responsibility.

sections.title: Tool and Equipment Recommendations
sections.body: The College advises the Manufacturing Service and other Services on tool and equipment acquisition, maintenance, and replacement. Recommendations are advisory unless the Assembly delegates decision-making authority.
sections.rationale: Practitioners know what tools work and what doesn't. Their input prevents wasteful purchasing and ensures Services maintain functional capacity.

sections.title: Quality Review
sections.body: The College may review the quality of fabrication work produced within community Services when concerns are raised. Quality review serves to identify training needs, process improvements, and standards compliance, not to assign blame.
sections.rationale: Peer review maintains quality while protecting the community interest in reliable work. Framing review as improvement-focused prevents it from becoming punitive.

sections.title: Annual Report
sections.body: The College shall publish an annual report covering: membership count and new admissions, apprenticeships in progress, knowledge-sharing activities, oversight committee work, safety incidents and responses, and standards revisions. The report shall be presented to the General Assembly.
sections.rationale: Transparency maintains accountability and gives the community visibility into the College's health and activity.

sections.title: Assembly Authority
sections.body: The General Assembly retains full authority over the College. It may revise this founding document, modify the College's domain, review membership decisions, or dissolve the College if it fails to serve community needs. College autonomy exists at the Assembly's discretion.
sections.rationale: Colleges must never become independent power centers. Community sovereignty is preserved through Assembly oversight.

sections.title: Member Appeals
sections.body: Any Society member denied College membership may appeal to the General Assembly. The Assembly shall determine whether the College followed its own criteria and whether those criteria are legitimate. The Assembly may direct admission if criteria were misapplied or are found to be exclusionary beyond what competence and safety require.
sections.rationale: Appeal rights prevent Colleges from becoming closed shops and ensure community access to qualified sortition pools.
